facts.statement: The genus Antarctosaurus was described by Friedrich von Huene in 1929.
facts.quote: authority: von Huene, 1929

facts.statement: Antarctosaurus fossils date to the Late Cretaceous Period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous,

facts.statement: The type species A. wichmannianus and the second species A. giganteus were both described by Friedrich von Huene in 1929.
facts.quote: The type species, Antarctosaurus wichmannianus, and a second species, Antarctosaurus giganteus, were described by prolific German paleontologist Friedrich von Huene in 1929.

facts.statement: Antarctosaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur that lived in South America during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Antarctosaurus (; meaning "southern lizard") is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Period of what is now South America.

facts.statement: Researchers are uncertain whether the remains attributed to the type species A. wichmannianus belong to the same individual or even the same genus.
facts.quote: The type species, A. wichmannianus, is controversial because there is uncertainty as to whether all the described remains belong to the same individual or even genus.

facts.statement: Remains of Antarctosaurus were first mentioned in print in 1916 but were not fully described until 1929.
facts.quote: Remains of this dinosaur were first mentioned in print in 1916, although they were not fully described and named until a 1929 monograph written by paleontologist Friedrich von Huene.

facts.statement: The name Antarctosaurus refers to the animal's location in Argentina, not the continent of Antarctica.
facts.quote: Antarctosaurus does not refer to the continent of Antarctica since it was first found in Argentina

facts.statement: The species A. wichmannianus was named in 1929 after Ricardo Wichmann, who discovered the remains in 1912.
facts.quote: Antarctosaurus wichmannianus is the type species of the genus, named in 1929 after the discoverer of its remains in 1912, geologist Ricardo Wichmann.

facts.statement: Fossils of A. wichmannianus come from the Anacleto Formation in Argentina, which is probably early Campanian in age.
facts.quote: which are considered to come from the Anacleto Formation in Río Negro Province of Argentina, which is probably early Campanian in age.

facts.statement: Two limb bones found in Chubut Province in 1924 were referred to A. wichmannianus by von Huene in 1929.
facts.quote: Two additional limb bones, found in the Chubut Province in 1924, were also referred to A. wichmannianus by von Huene in 1929.

facts.statement: Fossils of A. giganteus were recovered from the Plottier Formation in Neuquén Province, dating to the Coniacian-Santonian stages.
facts.quote: These fossils were recovered in Neuquén Province of Argentina, from the Plottier Formation, which dates to the Coniacian-Santonian stages of the Late Cretaceous Period.

facts.statement: Some researchers regard A. giganteus as a nomen dubium due to the scarcity of remains.
facts.quote: Very few remains are known of this species and it is regarded as a nomen dubium by some.

facts.statement: Other researchers consider A. giganteus a valid species but likely belonging to a new genus.
facts.quote: Other researchers regard A. giganteus as a likely valid species but probably belonging to a new genus.

facts.statement: In 1969, Leigh Van Valen hypothesized that A. wichmannianus and A. giganteus were growth stages of the same species.
facts.quote: In 1969, Leigh Van Valen considered A. wichmannianus and A. giganteus to be growth stages of the same species and favored the name A. giganteus.

facts.statement: Antarctosaurus septentrionalis was described by Von Huene and Charles Matley in 1933.
facts.quote: In 1933, Von Huene and Charles Matley described another species, Antarctosaurus septentrionalis, meaning "northern".

facts.statement: Remains of A. septentrionalis were found in the Lameta Formation of Madhya Pradesh, India.
facts.quote: The remains were found in the Lameta Formation of Madhya Pradesh State in India.

facts.statement: A. septentrionalis was assigned to the genus Jainosaurus in 1994.
facts.quote: This species does preserve important anatomical information but has since been assigned to its own genus in 1994; Jainosaurus.

facts.statement: A. jaxarticus from Kazakhstan is known only from a single femur.
facts.quote: Antarctosaurus jaxarticus from Kazakhstan is known from a single femur.

facts.statement: A. jaxarticus was named by Anatoly Riabinin in 1938.
facts.quote: It was named by Soviet paleontologist Anatoly Riabinin in 1938

facts.statement: Researchers have debated whether A. jaxarticus is a valid titanosaur, a nomen dubium, or a nomen nudum.
facts.quote: Other researchers have considered it as either, Titanosauridae incertae sedis, as a nomen dubium, or as a nomen nudum.

facts.statement: Fossils found in Brazil were described as A. brasiliensis in 1971.
facts.quote: In 1971 as A. brasiliensis.

facts.statement: Describing Antarctosaurus is problematic because no species is known from complete remains and the association of bones is questionable.
facts.quote: Describing Antarctosaurus is problematic because the type species consists of elements that are of questionable association and none of the species described are known from complete remains, which has caused a confused taxonomy of the genus.

facts.statement: The described remains belong to sauropods, likely titanosaurs, which were large, quadrupedal herbivores with long necks and tails.
facts.quote: The remains that have been described belong to sauropods, most probably titanosaurs, a group of large-bodied, quadrupedal herbivores, usually possessing a long neck and tail, with a small head.

facts.statement: The fossil remains of Antarctosaurus wichmannianus were assigned the specimen number MACN 6904.
facts.quote: The assemblage of fossil remains that became known as A. wichmannianus were given the specimen number MACN 6904.

facts.statement: The known fossils of A. wichmannianus include skull fragments, a neck vertebra, a tail vertebra, ribs, and limb bones, including a femur 1.39 meters tall.
facts.quote: The known material includes several skull fragments, including a braincase and an incomplete mandible (lower jaw), a cervical (neck) vertebra, a caudal (tail) vertebra, rib fragments, and numerous limb bones including a femur which measures 1.39 m tall.

facts.statement: No single fossil was designated as the holotype for A. wichmannianus, making MACN 6904 an assemblage of syntypes.
facts.quote: None of the individual fossils were designated the holotype specimen so MACN 6904 is considered to be an assemblage of syntypes.

facts.statement: The total estimated length of Antarctosaurus wichmannianus is around 17 meters.
facts.quote: The total length of A. wichmannianus has been estimated at around 17 m.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the squared-off jaws of A. wichmannianus indicate specialized feeding habits, possibly involving low vegetation or floating plants.
facts.quote: The squared-off jaws suggest specialised feeding habits, such as feeding near a surface plane like low vegetation on the ground or floating plants in water.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the square lower jaw of A. wichmannianus belongs to the species or to a rebbachisaurid sauropod similar to Nigersaurus.
facts.quote: In particular, the very square lower jaw has frequently been suggested to belong to a rebbachisaurid sauropod similar to Nigersaurus.

facts.statement: Except for an incomplete neck vertebra and a questionable tail vertebra, no vertebrae link the skull and limb bones of A. wichmannianus.
facts.quote: With the exception of an incomplete cervical vertebra and the questionable first caudal, there are no vertebrae that link the skull to the limb material.

facts.statement: Researchers usually regard the skull and skeleton of A. wichmannianus as titanosaurian, though they may not belong to the same individual.
facts.quote: The back of the skull and the remainder of the skeleton are usually regarded as titanosaurian by researchers, although they do not necessarily belong to the same type of titanosaur.

facts.statement: In 2005, Jeffrey Wilson suggested the braincase of A. wichmannianus might belong to the family Nemegtosauridae.
facts.quote: In 2005, Jeffrey Wilson considered the braincase as being referable to Nemegtosauridae but noted that other skull remains require further study.

facts.statement: The brain endocast and inner ear of A. wichmannianus share features with other titanosaurids, including short olfactory tracts and horizontally projected olfactory bulbs.
facts.quote: The brain endocast and inner ear share several features with other titanosaurids such as short olfactory tracts and olfactory bulbs that are horizontally projected.

facts.statement: Friedrich von Huene described a caudal vertebra of A. wichmannianus that was found near the skull material.
facts.quote: Von Huene described a caudal vertebra which was found close to the skull material.

facts.statement: Von Huene assigned two ankle bones, an astragalus and a calcaneum, to A. wichmannianus.
facts.quote: Von Huene assigned two tarsal (ankle) bones to A. wichmannianus, which he described as an astragalus and a calcanium.

facts.statement: The first caudal vertebra of A. wichmannianus features a biconvex centrum, a trait shared with other titanosaurs.
facts.quote: The vertebra features a biconvex centrum, a feature shared with other titanosaurs.

facts.statement: The femurs of Antarctosaurus giganteus measure 2.35 meters in length, among the largest of any known sauropod.
facts.quote: The two gigantic femora measure 2.35 m in length, which are among the largest of any known sauropod.

facts.statement: A 1956 reconstruction by Carlos Rusconi estimated the length of A. giganteus at around 30 meters.
facts.quote: A reconstruction of A. giganteus, published in 1956 by Carlos Rusconi, was given a length around 30 m.

facts.statement: In 1994, Gregory S. Paul estimated A. giganteus weighed between 80 and 100 metric tons and measured 30 to 35 meters long.
facts.quote: In 1994, Gregory S. Paul estimated the weight of both A. giganteus and Argentinosaurus at between 80 and 100 MT and lengths of 30 to 35 m long.

facts.statement: Based on some estimates, A. giganteus is considered among the heaviest known land animals.
facts.quote: This would make A. giganteus among the heaviest known land animals.

facts.statement: A 2016 study estimated the weight of A. giganteus at 39.5 metric tons based on limb bone circumference.
facts.quote: In 2016, using equations that estimate body mass based on the circumference of the humerus and femur of quadrupedal animals, it was estimated to be 39.5 MT in weight.

facts.statement: In 2020, Molina-Pérez and Larramendi estimated the length of A. giganteus at 30.5 meters and its weight at 45 metric tons.
facts.quote: In 2020 Molina-Pérez and Larramendi estimated its length at 30.5 m and its weight similar to Paul's estimation at 45 MT.

facts.statement: Despite their large size, the femurs of A. giganteus are somewhat gracile in construction.
facts.quote: Even though the femurs are large, they are also somewhat gracile in construction.

facts.statement: The type specimen of A. giganteus (MLP 26-316) includes femurs, pubis bones, a damaged tibia, ribs, tail vertebrae fragments, and six unidentifiable bones.
facts.quote: The type specimen of A. giganteus, MLP 26-316, includes a left and right femur, a partial left and right pubis, the distal end of a damaged tibia, numerous rib and distal caudal vertebrae fragments, and six large and unidentifiable bones.

facts.statement: Antarctosaurus jaxarticus is known only from a single femur that resembles one attributed to Jainosaurus.
facts.quote: "Antarctosaurus" jaxarticus is known from a single femur which was briefly reported as resembling a femur attributed to Jainosaurus (then called "Antarctosaurus" septentrionalis).

facts.statement: Antarctosaurus brasiliensis is known from three fragmentary titanosaurian bones: a partial femur, a partial humerus, and an incomplete dorsal vertebra.
facts.quote: "Antarctosaurus" brasiliensis is only known from three fragmentary bones that are titanosaurian in nature; a partial left femur GP-RD-2, a partial right humerus GP-RD-3, and an incomplete dorsal vertebra (backbone) GP-RD-4.

facts.statement: The preserved femur of A. brasiliensis is 1.15 meters long, estimated to be 1.55 meters if complete.
facts.quote: The femur is 1.15 m preserved and was estimated at 1.55 m if it were completed.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses place Antarctosaurus as a sister taxon to Vahiny and Jainosaurus, close to the clade Lognkosauria.
facts.quote: Antarctosaurus placed as sister taxon to a clade of Vahiny and Jainosaurus, consistently close to taxa of the clade Lognkosauria.

facts.statement: The type species of Antarctosaurus measured up to 18 meters in length and weighed around 34 tons.
facts.quote: La especie tipo de Antactosaurus medía hasta 18 metros de largo y alrededor de 34 toneladas de peso

facts.statement: A second, larger species is known from isolated remains, with a proposed size range of 23 to 30 meters in length.
facts.quote: Se conoce una segunda especie más grande, a partir de restos aislados, el rango propuesto de su tamaño sería de 23 a 30 metros de largo

facts.statement: Antarctosaurus was an enormous quadruped with long neck and tail, featuring osteoderms on its back.
facts.quote: Enorme cuadrúpedo de cuello y cola largas que presentaba osteodermos en su lomo

facts.statement: Its square-shaped lower jaw is particularly controversial.
facts.quote: Particularmente polémica es su mandíbula inferior que tenía una forma cuadrada

facts.statement: It had thin hind legs, large eyes, and a broad snout, but only a small head about 60 centimeters long with only a few peg-like teeth at the front.
facts.quote: Tenía piernas traseras delgadas, los ojos grandes y hocico amplio, pero solamente una pequeña cabeza de alrededor de 60 centímetros de largo con solamente algunos dientes como clavija en el frente

facts.statement: Remains of this dinosaur were first named in a 1916 publication but were not described and named until 1929 by Friedrich von Huene.
facts.quote: Los restos de este dinosaurio fueron nombrados por primera vez en una publicación de 1916, pero no fue descrito y nombrado hasta 1929 por Friedrich von Huene

facts.statement: The name does not come from Antarctica but from ancient Greek, meaning "reptile of the south" (anti-arktos-saurus).
facts.quote: El nombre no viene dado por la Antártida, sino que proviene del griego antiguo anti, que significa "contrario de" y arktos, que significa deducidamente "al norte" y saurus también del griego que habla de su naturaleza reptil

facts.statement: Von Huene named A. wichmannianus in honor of geologist Ricardo Wichmann, who discovered the remains in 1912.
facts.quote: Von Huene uso el nombre A. wichmannianus, que toma su nombre en honor al descubridor de sus restos en 1912, el geólogo Ricardo Wichmann

facts.statement: The remains are now considered to come from the Anacleto Formation in Río Negro Province, Argentina.
facts.quote: que ahora se consideran provenientes de Formación Anacleto en la provincia de Río Negro en Argentina

facts.statement: Two additional limb bones found in Chubut Province in 1924 were also referred to A. wichmannianus by von Huene in 1929.
facts.quote: Dos huesos de extremidades adicionales, encontrados en la provincia de Chubut en 1924, también fueron referidos a A. wichmannianus por von Huene en 1929

facts.statement: Remains of A. wichmannianus are also known from the Ascencio Formation in Uruguay and the Vinitos Formation in Chile.
facts.quote: Se conocen también restos de A. wichmannianus provenientes de la Formación Ascencio, Departamento de Tacuarembó en Uruguay, y en la Formación Vinitos, de la Provincia de Coquimbo, Chile

facts.statement: A second fragmentary species was tentatively named cf. Antarctosaurus giganteus by von Huene in 1929 due to its enormous size.
facts.quote: Una segunda especie fragmentaria de Antarctosaurus fue descrita por von Huene en la misma monografía de 1929, que tentativamente llamó cf. Antarctosaurus giganteus por su enorme tamaño

facts.statement: This second species is based on remains from the Plottier Formation in Neuquén Province, dating to the Coniacian, 87 to 85 million years ago.
facts.quote: Se basa en restos encontrados en la Formación Plottier, levemente más antigua, en el Coniaciense hace 87 a 85 millones de años, en la Provincia del Neuquén

facts.statement: In 1933, von Huene and Charles Matley described A. septentrionalis, found in the Lameta Formation in Madhya Pradesh, India.
facts.quote: En 1933 von Huene y Charles Matley, describen a A. septentrionalis, que significa "norteño". Los restos fueron encontrados en la Formación Lameta del estado de Madhya Pradesh en India

facts.statement: In 1939, Anatoly Riabinin described A. jaxarticus based on a single femur from what is now Kazakhstan.
facts.quote: En 1939 Anatoly Riabinin describe A. jaxarticus por un solo fémur, proveniente de lo que es hoy Kazajistán

facts.statement: The last named species, A. brasilensis, comes from Brazil and was named in 1971.
facts.quote: La última especie nombrada en 1971 proviene de Brasil, A. brasilensis

facts.statement: In 1970, fragmentary limb bones and a partial vertebra were found in the Adamantina Formation.
facts.quote: En 1970, se encontraron dos huesos fragmentarios de las extremidades y una vértebra parcial en la Formación Adamantina

facts.statement: The remains were described by discoverers Fahad Moysés Arid and Luiz Dino Vizotto in 1971 as A. brasiliensis.
facts.quote: Los restos fueron descritos por sus descubridores Fahad Moysés Arid y Luiz Dino Vizotto en 1971 como A. brasiliensis

facts.statement: A. wichmannianus has been considered a Lithostrotia, a group including armored titanosaurs, although no shield was associated with the remains.
facts.quote: A. wichmannianus se ha considerado como un Lithostrotia un grupo que incluye titanosáuridos acorazados, aunque no se asociara ningún escudo a los restos

facts.statement: The type species was placed as a possible nemegtosaurine.
facts.quote: La especie tipo fue colocada como un posible nemegtosaurínido

facts.statement: It is debated whether the square jaw shape is a convergence with rebbachisaurids or truly belongs to Antarctosaurus, as the recent discovery of Bonitasaura suggests the latter.
facts.quote: aunque el descubrimiento reciente del titanosaurio Bonitasaura sugiere que quizá la convergencia en estilo de la mandíbula entre los rebaquisáuridos y los titanosaurios que esta pertenezca al Antarctosaurus realmente

facts.statement: In 1969, Leigh Van Valen considered A. wichmannianus and A. giganteus to be growth stages of the same species, favoring the name A. giganteus.
facts.quote: En 1969, Leigh Van Valen consideró que A. wichmannianus y A. giganteus eran etapas de crecimiento de la misma especie y favoreció el nombre de A. giganteus

facts.statement: This idea is problematic because A. wichmannianus was named earlier in the same article and is known from more material, so it should have priority over A. giganteus.
facts.quote: Esta idea es problemática porque A. wichmannianus fue nombrado anteriormente en el mismo artículo y se conoce por más material, por lo que debería tener prioridad sobre A. giganteus

facts.statement: The two species do not belong to the same geological formation, suggesting they did not belong to the same time period.
facts.quote: Las dos especies tampoco pertenecen a la misma formación geológica, lo que sugiere que no pertenecieron al mismo período de tiempo

facts.statement: A. giganteus may have been one of the largest dinosaurs discovered, estimated to reach 23 to 30 meters in length and weigh 69 tons.
facts.quote: Antarctosaurus giganteus pudo haber sido uno de los mayores dinosaurios descubiertos, llegando a medir entre 23 y 30 metros de largo y pesar 69 toneladas según los estimados

facts.statement: The species Antarctosaurus giganteus was described by Von Heune in 1929.
facts.quote: Segunda especie de antarctosaurio descripta por Von Heune en el año 1929 y llamada A. giganteus por su gran tamaño.

facts.statement: Fossils of Antarctosaurus were found in Neuquén, Argentina, in the Plottier Formation dating to the Late Cretaceous, 88 to 86 million years ago.
facts.quote: Los huesos fósiles se encontraron en Neuquén, Argentina en la Formación Plottier que data del periodo Cretácico superior hace 88 a 86 millones de años.

facts.statement: The most notable known remains are two femurs measuring 2.35 meters in length, among the largest known for any dinosaur.
facts.quote: Lo más destacable de los pocos restos conocidos, son dos fémures gigantes de 2,35 m de largo, los cuales están entre los más grandes conocidos para un dinosaurio.

facts.statement: Based on the study of its remains, Antarctosaurus giganteus is estimated to have been 23 to 30 meters long and weighed about 69 tons.
facts.quote: Tras su estudio, se estima que el animal completo habría medido entre 23 y 30 m de largo y pesado unas 69 toneladas, apenas un poco menos que las 73 toneladas estimadas para el gigante Argentinosaurus, uno de los mayores dinosaurios conocidos.

facts.statement: The species Antarctosaurus septentrionalis was described by Von Heune in 1933 based on very poor remains from India.
facts.quote: Descripta por Von Heune en 1933 en la India, los restos son muy pobres, y se tiene una descripción incompleta del mismo.

facts.statement: Antarctosaurus septentrionalis was reassigned to its own genus, Jainosaurus, in 1994.
facts.quote: Ha sido reubicada en su propio género Jainosaurus en 1994.

facts.statement: The species Antarctosaurus jaxartensis is known from a single femur found in Kazakhstan by Anatoly Riabinin in 1939.
facts.quote: Conocido por un único fémur encontrado en Kazajistán por Anatoly Riabinin en 1939.

facts.statement: The fossils of Antarctosaurus jaxartensis date between 93.5 and 83.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Los restos fósiles datan de entre 93,5 y 83,5 millones años atrás.

facts.statement: Fragmentary remains of Antarctosaurus brasiliensis were found in the Bauru Formation in Brazil and described by Arid and Vizzotto in 1971.
facts.quote: Restos fragmentarios de este dinosaurio fueron encontrado en la Formación Bauru en Brasil y descriptas por Arid y Vizzotto en 1971.

facts.statement: The species Antarctosaurus brasiliensis is considered a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: Esta especie es considerada como nomen dubium.

facts.statement: Antarctosaurus is considered a derived Titanosauria within Lithostrotia, though some articles classify it as a Saltasauridae or Nemegtosaurinae.
facts.quote: Antarctosaurus es considerado un Titanosauria derivado, dentro de Lithostrotia, por lo menos un artículo lo considera un Saltasauridae, Nemegtosaurinae.

facts.statement: In phylogenetic analyses, Antarctosaurus is placed as the sister taxon to a clade containing Vahiny and Jainosaurus, consistently near the Lognkosauria clade.
facts.quote: Antarctosaurus colocado como taxón hermano de un clado de Vahiny y Jainosaurus , consistentemente cerca de los taxones del clado Lognkosauria.

facts.statement: The parent group of the genus Antarctosaurus is Lithostrotia.
facts.quote: Parent group: Lithostrotia

facts.statement: Antarctosaurus belongs to the class Saurischia.
facts.quote: Class: Saurischia

facts.statement: The genus Antarctosaurus lived from the Coniacian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 89.8 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Coniacian to Maastrichtian (89.8 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Due to the scarcity of remains, the exact size of Antarctosaurus giganteus is unknown, and some consider it a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: Debido a la escasez de restos, se desconoce su tamaño exacto. Segunda especie de antarctosaurio descripta por Von Heune en el año 1929 y llamada A. giganteus por su gran tamaño. se conocen muy pocos restos de este animal, por lo que es considerada nomen dubium por algunos.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Antarctosaurus giganteus can be confidently assigned to the genus Antarctosaurus due to the poor condition of the material and confusion with A. wichmannianus.
facts.quote: Por lo poco se sabe de este animal, y porque el material que se asignó a A. wichmannianus es tan confuso, A. giganteus puede no ser asignado con confianza al género Antarctosaurus actualmente.

facts.statement: Antarctosaurus jaxartensis is considered a nomen dubium today, but it is almost certainly not a species of the South American Antarctosaurus.
facts.quote: Es colocado como nomen dubium hoy, pero casi con certeza no es una especie del suramericano Antarctosaurus.
